title: Disaster Recovery Community Update Meeting #2 at Lahaina Civic Center: November 15, 2023

issues.title: Moving fire survivors off FEMA interim housing

recap.headline: Lahaina recovery update on water, wastewater, air quality, debris and housing
recap.in_60_seconds: County, State and federal officials held their second weekly disaster recovery update at the Lahaina Civic Center. Eight officials presented, and no residents spoke at the microphone; questions were taken at information tables. Officials said residential reentry should be finished by mid-December, drinking water should be restored to most of the system in three to six months, and FEMA has raised its rental assistance limit to 175% of fair market rent. Officials also explained debris removal sign-up and insurance, and how air quality is monitored at schools and in burn areas. No date was given for possible sewer service in Wahikuli, and soil sample results are still about three weeks away. The next meeting is next Wednesday.

parts.title: Welcome and introductions
presented: Weekly update meeting with several departments, set up around concerns raised the week before.
The West Maui council member and three Lahaina advisory members were acknowledged.

parts.title: Reentry and emergency alerts update
presented: Interpreters were available for several languages, and agency tables were set up on both sides of the room.
Reentry is more than halfway through residential properties, with a goal of finishing by mid-December; some reentries may be postponed for weather.
Getting people back into standing homes depends on water and wastewater service.
After a brush fire in Kīhei the day before, alerts may go only to the affected area; the agency is working more closely with radio stations.

parts.title: Water system restoration
parts.presenter: Deputy Director, Department of Water Supply
presented: Areas 1 and 2 are cleared as safe to drink.
Areas 3A and 3B are being worked on; 3B, the business area, is expected to be cleared next week.
Areas 4 and 4B need about two to three more weeks; crews will then move north and south, starting with areas that have the most standing homes.
Clearing most of the system may take three to six months because of testing, flushing and repairs to hydrants, mains, valves and service laterals.

next.what: Most of the water system cleared

parts.title: Wastewater system update
presented: Pump Station 4 was restored about two to three weeks after the fire; Pump Stations 5 and 6 were just restored, and Pump Station 7 appears to be working.
The Front Street trunk line is close to being back in service; areas from Leialiʻi Hawaiian Homes north are working.
The County is procuring a damage assessment of the system.
The County hopes to work with EPA to sewer Wahikuli so rebuilders would not need septic systems; no timing was given.

parts.title: School air quality
parts.presenter: Department of Education Complex Area Superintendent
presented: A 16-page safe and healthy guidance document for Lahaina schools was developed with the Department of Health, based on federal guidance.
Sensor changes can often be explained by local activity, such as blowers used to clean a track.
Families and staff will be notified right away through school messages and local media if there are concerns.
Wipe tests are done every two weeks inside and outside classrooms; the guidance can be downloaded from the Hawaiʻi Public Schools website.

parts.title: Air and soil monitoring
parts.presenter: Deputy Director for Environmental Health, State Department of Health
presented: Soil samples from homes have been sent to the lab, and results are expected in about three weeks.
There are 49 sensors and monitors on Maui and Lānaʻi, including 15 PurpleAir sensors and 5 E-BAMs in Lahaina and 25 sensors in Kula.
Staff were sent to install about 8 more sensors.
A contractor began air monitoring at three Kula sites, including about 10 days of continuous asbestos and heavy metals monitoring.

next.what: Soil sample results reported to the public

parts.title: Fire debris removal and right of entry
presented: Owners who want the government program to clean their property must submit a right of entry form, online at mauirecovers.org or with help at the County building lobby or the Lahaina Disaster Recovery Center.
The form includes a sketch for marking cesspools, septic systems, rock walls or special trees to protect.
If insurance has a dollar amount for debris removal, the County may ask for that amount and nothing more; owners who do their own cleanup pay for it themselves.
The Army Corps of Engineers, Tidal Basin and historic and cultural monitoring teams were available at tables; staff can help with trusts and shared titles.

parts.title: FEMA housing update
presented: The goal is to get everyone into safe, secure housing by the end of the year.
FEMA is seeking owners to lease vacation homes, rentals or apartments to survivors for up to 18 months.
84 units have been secured, and 10 survivors have been housed in them.
Rental assistance limits were raised from 100% to 175% of fair market rent; a two-bedroom goes from $2,070 to $3,622.

next.what: Everyone in safe and secure housing

parts.title: Meeting format and info tables
presented: Residents were asked to suggest changes to the meeting format and which presenters they want next time.
Presenters were available at tables for one-on-one questions.

parts.title: Mayor's closing remarks
presented: The mayor said policies apply to groups, so residents should bring their own situations to the tables.

Signing up for Army Corps debris removal is a personal choice with no out-of-pocket cost, though insurance debris coverage may have to be given to the government; 26 homes were given as an example of signed rights of entry.
The mayor said going back to work and sending children to school are personal choices.

open_questions.question: When could Wahikuli get sewer service so rebuilders do not need septic systems?
Who exactly receives a homeowner's insurance debris removal payment when the government cleans the property?

not_on_tracker.why: Residents with standing homes cannot move back until their water is cleared as safe.

not_on_tracker.topic: Fire debris removal sign-up and insurance
not_on_tracker.why: Property owners need to decide on right of entry and know what it will cost before cleanup can start.
Parents asked the week before how children are being kept safe from smoke and dust near the burn area.

moments.quote: With that, we're currently seeking property owners here in Hawaii who want to temporarily lease their vacation homes, rentals, and or apartments. Please visit our FEMA staff over there to get an email address if you have a property that you want to rent to a survivor for up to 18 months.
moments.about: Shows how FEMA's interim housing for fire survivors began in November 2023, with leases of up to 18 months, which is the housing survivors are now being moved off of.
